August 20, 1913. Mr. Charles M. McCabe may be reinstated as a clerk in the Postal Service without reference to the year limitation of the reinstatement rule. Mr. McCabe was removed from the Nashville, Tenn., post, office on September 10, 1898, notice of his removal alleging ‘‘inefficiency.”” No charge of inefficiency had been preferred against him and he was allowed no opportunity to reply to the charge as required by the rules then in effect. Mr. McCabe as a member of the board of civil service examiners for the Nashville post office rendered assistance to the commission in connection with investigations involving the collector of internal revenue, who was removed by the President for violation of the civil service rules. The Postmaster General states that it appears that Mr. McCabe was removed on political grounds, and the issuance of an Executive order for his reinstaterient seems to be justified by the facts in the case. In view of the facts stated above the Civil Service Commission concurs in recom- mending this order.

July 6, 1914. Capt. James Lee Cochrun may be appointed to a position as field agent in the Deperiment of Agriculture without reference to the requirements of the civil-service rules. Capt. Cochrun, who has been an officer in the Philippine Constabulary since Novem- ber 26, 1906, rendered exceptionally meritorious service, was seriously and painfully wounded in an engagement, with hostile Moros on January 23, 1913, and has received a medal for valor, He is incapacitated for further service as a constabulary officer, but is fully able to perform the duties of the position to which the Department of Agriculture desires to appoint bim. Under an Executive order of August 12, 1907, an officer of the Philippine Constab- ulary who has served seven years or more may be classified, in cases of exceptional merit, for appointment to the Federal classified service. By virtue of this order the Civil Service Commission, on May 21, 1914, upon the recommendation of the War Department, gave Capt. Cochrun a classified status, and subsequently authorized his transfer, without examination, to a position as clerk in the Bureau of Insular Affairs. In view of the fact that there is no vacancy in that bureau to which Capt. Cochrun could be appointed the Secretary of War and the Secretary of Agriculture recommend that he be transferred and appointed to the position of field agent in the Department of Agriculture.

August 26, 1915. The year limit upon eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit the reinstatement of Green A. Stephens in the postal service. Mr. Stephens was a carrier in the San Francisco post office from June 23, 1891, to April 12, 1905, when he was removed upon the charge of tampering with mail addressed to a patron in his district and using a race-track admission ticket contained in a letter so addressed. A careful reinvestigation by a post-office inspector resulted in the con- clusion that beyond any reasonable doubt Mr. Stephens was not guilty of the charge for which he was removed from the postal service. The Postmaster General states that there is no question in his mind but that a distinct injustice was done in separating Carrier Stephens from the service on the flimsy and prejudiced evidence which was adduced in the case. He therefore recommends that an Executive order be issued to reinstate him in the service, and the Civil Service Commission, after careful review of the case, concurs in this recommendation.

It appears that there is a real necessity for a competent and experienced woman in connection with the detention and deportation of this class of aliens. March 29, 1926. Mr. Thomas Howard Bailey may be employed as watchman in the office of the Director of Public Buildings and Public Parks of the National Capital without regard to the civil service act and rules. Mr. Bailey was injured in a powder explosion in the line of his duty in a turret of the U. S. S. Trenton. The Secretary of the Navy, in recommending this order, says: "Mr. Bailey was jammed in the rear access door, pinned there by reason of the fact that his leg was doubled up in the pile of unconscious men around the hand rammer, and, although the skin from his face and hands was hanging in shreds from severe burns, he succeeded in getting the nozzle of the hose and passing it into the turret, thereafter keeping the kinks out of it where it passed over the edge of the door. Although so seriously wounded, he repeat- edly refused assistance for himself until several of the other men had been cleared away and passed to safety. He was honorably discharged on February 6, 1925, on account of physical disability incurred in the line of duty. This disability also prevents Mr. Bailey from securifig sufficiently remunerative com- mercial employment." The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending the order in recogni- tion of the heroic conduct of Mr. Bailey. Mr. Bailey entered the service as a laborer on September 3, 1908.

March 30, 1916. Mr. Herbert D. Dean may be reinstated as a fish culturist in the Bureau of Fisheries, Department of Commerce, without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. Mr. Dean entered the service of the Bureau of Fisheries in a subordinate capacity in 1884 and in 1891, after four promo- tions, became a superintendent of station, which position, with the exception of five months in 1895, he held until March 11, 1912, when, at his own request, his services were discontinued without prejudice. Mr. Dean‘s record was satis- factory, and he was generally recognized as an efficient fish culturist and super- intendent. This order is issued upon recommendation of the Secretary of Com- merce, who is of the opinion that Mr. Dean’s reentrance into the fisheries service will be beneficial thereto, and who therefore believes that an exception to the one-year limitation in cases of separation from the service imposed by civil- service Rule IX is justified and advisable. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation.

Mrs. Walker has also had service in the Census Office.

October 14, 1915. Mr. William H. H. Bowen may be reinstated in the field service of tthe Internal Revenue Service without regard to the year limit required by the civil- service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. The Secre- tary of the Treasury states that Mr. Bowen served very efficiently in the Internal Revenue Service for 19 years and resigned from the position of in- ternal revenue agent to accept the appointment of postmaster at Covington, Ky., retiring from that position on September 1, 1914; that the records of the department show that the work performed by Mr. Bowen as internal revenue agent was of an unusually efficient character ; and the Internal Revenue Service at this time is in need of such men as Mr. Bowen, men who are able to take up successfully any and every phase of the internal revenue work. Mr. Bowen, ‘acting on information inadvertently given by a commissioner, failed to make application for reinstatement in the Internal Revenue Service before the ex- piration of the year limit, required by the rules.

March 30, 1914. Mr. James L. Murphy may be retransferred to an appropriate position in the competi- tive classified service. Mr. Murphy was in the service of the Interstate Commerce Commission from July 10, 1893, to February 10, 1911, and was deputy marshal of the Commerce Court from the latter date to December 31, 1913, when the court was abolished by law. Under the civil-service rules any person may be retransferred to a position in which he was formerly employed or to any position to which transfer could be made therefrom if since his transfer he has been continuously in the executive or judicial civil service of the United States and the commission may waive the requirement of six months’ service immediately preceding transfer where the person has been separated within the year on account of necessary reduction of force and not by inefficiency. It is no fault of Mr. Murphy that he is not entitled to this privilege. He lost his position through the abolition of the Commerce Court. This order, which meets the approval of the Civil Service Commission, merely accords to Mr. Murphy the privilege he would have had if he had been separated from a competitive position under like circum- stances.

July 28, 1916. Mrs. Olga S. Moncure may be reinstated in the position of topographic draftsman in the Coast and Geodetic Survey, Department of Commerce, with- out regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the superintendent of the survey, who state that Mrs. Moncure served satisfactorily and very efficiently in a statutory position of topographic draftsman in the Geological Survey during a period of seven years; that upon applying for a short leave of absence she was transferred to a position on a per diem, when actually em- ployed, basis with the positive assurance of her superior officers that such transfer would not deprive her of her status in the classified civil service; that she did apply for restoration to duty prior to the expiration of the time during which she was advised that she would be eligible for such return to duty and then learned that she had been misinformed, and as a result of the action of her superiors she lost her civil-service status; that she later obtained a position of draftsman in the bureau of lands in the Philippines and while serving in that capacity was detailed for work under the director of coast surveys at Manila, who has certified to her faithfulness, efficiency, and atten- tion to duty; and that in view of these circumstances it is believed that her reinstatement in the Coast and Geodetic Survey is fully justified and desirable in the interests of good administration and will remedy a manifest injustice which has been done in her case.

December 26, 1917, Frederick S. Taylor may be appointed to a subclerical position in the classified service of the Treasury Department without compliance with the requirements of the Civil Service Commission. : This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Taylor has considerable knowledge of photography and that it is desired to use his services in a low-salaried position as an assistant to the official photographer in the Office of the Supervising Architect, and it is believed the appointment will be in the interest of the service.

October 17, 1913. Mr. William J. Levy may be reinstated as a clerk in the Treasury Department without compliance with civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury in view of Mr. Levy’s former efficient service in the Treasury Department, where he proved to be an exceptionally able and expert technical bookkeeper. His services in that line are especially desired now because of the new accounting system inaugu- rated in that department. The needs of the office of the Treasurer of the United States at the present time are unusual and extraordinary, and Mr. Levy possesses special and peculiar qualifications as a technical bookkeeper.

January 7, 1915. It is hereby ordered that the physical requirements be waived in order that Mr. George P. Kinsman, of the battleship Vermont, who lost his right leg as the result of injuries sustained during the occupation of Vera Cruz by the American troops in April, 1914, may take the clerk-carrier examination in the postal service.

March 29, 1917. Mr. Claude T. Worford may be appointed to the ositon of draftsman at $1,200 per annum in the Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department, without regard to the civil-service rules. Efforts of the Navy Department to fill this vacancy by certification and by transfer have failed. The work is represented as confidential and secret to the highest degree, ‘and the Secretary of the Navy states that it is imperative that the office should know in advance the qualifications, antecedents, affiliations, and sympathies of the ap- pointee. He states that Mr. Worford possesses the necessary qualifications, and has to his credit four years of service in the Navy with an honorable discharge and a good conduct medal. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Secretary of the Navy in recom- mending this order.
